newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Peacekeepers tell Liberia faction to free rivals.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers tell Liberia faction to free rivals.

text.p: Gunmen in Liberia have taken hostage two commanders from a rival faction who were on a U.N.-sponsored ceasefire monitoring mission, threatening to derail the latest peace process, diplomats said.

The head of the West African peacekeeping force in Liberia, which also took part in the mission, ordered the immediate release of the two on Wednesday, denouncing their seizure the day before as a breach of a peace deal agreed in August.

General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led force, told George Boley's ethnic Krahn Liberia Peace Council at the same time to return property seized from other members of the ceasefire monitoring team to southeast Liberia.

"This act on the part of the LPC is a gross violation of the Abuja Accord," Malu told reporters after talks on Wednesday among peacekeepers, U.N. and faction representatives one day after the two were taken hostage in the town of Zwedru.
U.N. special envoy Anthony Nyakyi of Tanzania described the seizure as "a serious threat to the peace process".

A Western diplomat who travelled with the truce monitoring team told reporters quick action was necessary to prevent the incident derailing the latest peace deal, which West African leaders brokered in Nigeria's capital Abuja in August.
"If nothing is done, that's the end of Abuja," he said.

Members of the mission said on their return to the capital Monrovia late on Tuesday that two generals of the National Patriotic Front of Liberia had been seized as they left a U.N. helicopter in Zwedru.
Peace Council fighters had robbed helicopter crew members and peacekeepers, taking cash, ammunition and communications equipment, they added.
Peacekeeping sources had said earlier that peacekeepers had won a pledge that the two hostages, generals John Tarnue and Francis Dolo, would be freed.
The two men are supporters of Charles Taylor, the man who launched the civil war in December 1989. The factions have traded allegations of truce violations in the south east.
The peace deal, backed up by the threat of individual sanctions against any faction leader undermining the process, envisages disarmament by January and elections in May.

The war has killed well over 150,000 people. The truce followed fighting that killed hundreds of people in Monrovia in April and May. The United States sent in Marines to protect its embassy and airlifted out U.S. and other foreign nationals.
